frictionVectors.title: European gas dependence
frictionVectors.details: Europe remains a major market for Algerian pipeline and LNG exports, creating bargaining leverage but also exposure to shifting demand, pricing, and external pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon concentration
frictionVectors.details: Strong state control over oil and gas supports sovereignty, but fiscal and foreign-exchange dependence on hydrocarbons limits resilience and complicates diversification.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector dependence
frictionVectors.details: The state retains formal control over petroleum resources, but declining production, debt exposure, and reliance on foreign operators constrain effective sovereign leverage.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure finance
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed rail, energy, and construction projects expand connectivity while reinforcing creditor, contractor, and strategic dependence on outside partners.

frictionVectors.title: Cotonou-Niger trade rupture
frictionVectors.details: Political tensions with Niger have disrupted transit and exposed Benin's dependence on cross-border commerce, port access, and regional diplomatic stability.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-backed logistics expansion
frictionVectors.details: Investment in the Port of Cotonou and transport corridors is improving state capacity, but external financiers and operators retain significant influence over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers renegotiation pressure
frictionVectors.details: Botswana is seeking a larger share of diamond value and stronger domestic beneficiation, while prolonged market weakness tests the durability of its partnership with De Beers.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: New interest in copper, nickel, and other minerals could diversify the economy, but competition among foreign investors creates pressure to preserve regulatory and environmental autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector control struggle
frictionVectors.details: The government is pursuing greater control over gold production and mining revenues, but insecurity, informal extraction, and opaque licensing continue to weaken effective resource sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Security dependence on Russia
frictionVectors.details: The shift away from French and Western security ties toward Russian support increases political autonomy from former partners but creates new dependency risks and has not resolved militant violence.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda-Burundi security rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Mutual accusations over rebel support and border insecurity continue to constrain trade and regional coordination. Great Lakes tensions limit Burundi's room to pursue independent security partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals infrastructure gap
frictionVectors.details: Burundi is seeking foreign capital and logistics partnerships to develop nickel and rare-earth potential, but weak transport links and opaque contracting risk leaving value capture abroad.

frictionVectors.title: Port and maritime-security competition
frictionVectors.details: European, Chinese, and other external actors are competing for influence around ports, connectivity, and Atlantic maritime surveillance. Praia is balancing these relationships while protecting strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Tourism and energy exposure
frictionVectors.details: Heavy reliance on foreign tourists, imported fuel, and external infrastructure finance leaves the islands vulnerable to international shocks. Renewable-energy expansion improves resilience but remains incomplete.

highlights: Oil and minerals remain externally leveraged

frictionVectors.title: Chinese infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and construction remain important for roads, dams, and industrial projects, while debt, local-content concerns, and opaque procurement limit domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone conflict and resource access
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the Northwest and Southwest disrupts roads, agricultural production, and state access while creating openings for illicit taxation and outside arms networks.

highlights: Security partnerships trade access for protection

frictionVectors.title: Russian security-for-resources model
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security personnel retain influence around regime protection and mining interests, reducing transparency over concessions and weakening independent state oversight.

frictionVectors.title: Illicit gold and border corridors
frictionVectors.details: Gold, diamonds, and timber move through poorly governed borders toward neighboring markets, while armed groups and foreign commercial networks compete for transport routes and extraction sites.

highlights: Oil revenues underpin a centralized state

frictionVectors.title: Sudan spillover and foreign security ties
frictionVectors.details: The Sudan conflict drives refugee flows, arms trafficking, and cross-border insecurity, while competing Gulf and regional actors seek influence over Chad's security and logistics corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Oil dependence and pipeline vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon revenues remain concentrated in state institutions and exposed to production and export disruptions. Limited diversification weakens bargaining power with foreign operators and external financiers.

frictionVectors.title: French Control of Mayotte
frictionVectors.details: France retains control of Mayotte, sustaining a core sovereignty dispute and limiting Comoros' influence over surrounding maritime resources. Migration management and naval access keep the issue diplomatically active.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Reliance
frictionVectors.details: Comoros depends heavily on foreign donors and external partners for ports, energy, transport, and telecommunications. This creates leverage for outside actors over national infrastructure priorities.

frictionVectors.title: M23-Rwanda Security Nexus
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in eastern Congo continues to undermine state control over territory, mining zones, and transport corridors. Rwanda-linked armed networks and regional military involvement keep sovereignty highly contested.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Mining Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Western, and regional firms compete for access to cobalt, copper, gold, and other strategic minerals. Contract renegotiations and efforts to expand domestic processing have improved leverage but not eliminated asymmetry.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Oil remains central to state revenue and export earnings, exposing Congo to price shocks and constraining broader economic sovereignty. Foreign operators retain substantial technical and commercial influence in the sector.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-Linked Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-financed roads, ports, and public works have expanded connectivity while increasing dependence on external capital and contractors. The government retains political control, but fiscal constraints narrow its bargaining room.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Cocoa Processing
frictionVectors.details: Cote d'Ivoire is seeking more domestic processing and stronger producer returns, but multinational traders and processors still dominate financing, logistics, and global market access. This limits the country's ability to capture the full value of its leading export.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Strategic Investment Competition
frictionVectors.details: Abidjan and San Pedro attract French, Chinese, Gulf, and other foreign investment, strengthening infrastructure while creating competing external interests. The government has generally maintained policy control and diversified partnerships.

highlights: Ports at the Red Sea Chokepoint

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military Base Density
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti hosts major foreign military facilities, including U.S., Chinese, French, Japanese, and other deployments. Base rents provide revenue and diplomatic leverage but constrain strategic autonomy and heighten exposure to regional conflict.

frictionVectors.title: Port Debt and Strategic Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The port and logistics sector is central to Djibouti's economy and closely linked to external financing, especially Chinese-backed infrastructure. Debt exposure and competition over Red Sea access give foreign partners substantial influence over national assets.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: IMF requirements and Gulf investment provide essential foreign exchange but increase outside influence over strategic assets, privatization, and economic policy.

frictionVectors.title: Nile water confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The GERD dispute with Ethiopia remains unresolved, keeping Egypt focused on binding operating rules and limiting perceived risks to its water security.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon depletion
frictionVectors.details: Declining mature fields and limited new discoveries reduce fiscal room, increasing reliance on foreign operators, gas partnerships, and opaque production-sharing arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Port and gas competition
frictionVectors.details: The government is promoting LNG, petrochemicals, and maritime infrastructure while balancing Chinese, Western, and regional commercial interests around its ports and energy assets.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal revenues remain concentrated among a small number of foreign-linked projects, limiting domestic value capture and exposing the state to commodity and sanctions risk.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea militarization
frictionVectors.details: Assab and Massawa retain strategic value amid regional naval competition, but Eritrea's opaque security posture and ties with external military actors heighten sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Trade and fiscal dependence
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini remains heavily dependent on South African logistics, electricity, investment, and customs revenues, leaving its economic sovereignty vulnerable to Pretoria's market conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Textile preference exposure
frictionVectors.details: Textile and sugar sectors depend on external market access and trade preferences, especially with the United States and regional blocs, creating recurring infrastructure and policy pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Nile basin escalation
frictionVectors.details: The GERD strengthens Ethiopia's electricity and bargaining position, but unresolved operating arrangements with Egypt and Sudan keep water security at the center of regional tensions.

frictionVectors.title: Port-access competition
frictionVectors.details: Ethiopia's search for reliable Red Sea access intersects with Somali sovereignty concerns and competing Gulf, Turkish, Egyptian, and Emirati interests in the Horn.

highlights: Manganese and Oil at the Core

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Concession Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The post-Bongo government is seeking greater state value from oil, manganese, and timber concessions while preserving investment flows. Renegotiation risks tension with established French and multinational commercial interests.

frictionVectors.title: Rail and Port Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Mineral exports remain dependent on rail and port infrastructure vulnerable to financing, maintenance, and foreign-operator leverage. Limited domestic processing constrains Gabon's bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Fishing Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Weak monitoring capacity leaves coastal fisheries exposed to foreign fleets and opaque licensing arrangements. Fish-stock depletion directly threatens food security and local incomes.

frictionVectors.title: Transport and Port Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Trade depends heavily on the Port of Banjul and overland links through Senegal, giving Dakar substantial logistical leverage. Ferry and road bottlenecks continue to raise the cost of national commerce.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal Mining and Water Security
frictionVectors.details: Unregulated gold mining, including activity involving foreign-linked operators, continues to damage rivers and undermine state authority. Enforcement remains politically difficult because mining supports employment and local patronage networks.

frictionVectors.title: IMF and Creditor Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF-linked reforms limit fiscal room for infrastructure and industrial policy. Ghana is seeking more domestic processing of gold, cocoa, and critical minerals while remaining reliant on external finance.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou Rail and Port Leverage
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou project is reshaping Guinea's strategic position, but rail, port, and processing infrastructure is being developed through large foreign-backed consortia. Control over corridor access and revenue-sharing will remain a central sovereignty issue.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Guinea remains heavily dependent on foreign firms and external markets for bauxite extraction and logistics. The government is pressing for local processing and tighter oversight, creating friction with major Chinese, Gulf, and Western investors.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew Value-Chain Capture
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains concentrated in raw cashew exports, leaving farmers and the state exposed to foreign buyers, price swings, and weak domestic processing capacity. Seasonal trade disruptions quickly translate into political and fiscal stress.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime Security and Port Weakness
frictionVectors.details: Limited naval, customs, and port capacity creates space for illicit trafficking and opaque foreign fishing activity. Dependence on external security and commercial partners reduces Bissau's control over maritime resources.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt and Project Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Heavy debt-service obligations, including exposure to Chinese-linked infrastructure financing and IMF conditionality, constrain Nairobi's room to set independent fiscal and development priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: The Mombasa port and Northern Corridor remain strategic targets for Gulf, Chinese, and Western commercial interests, while Kenya faces pressure to balance regional integration with control over critical logistics assets.

frictionVectors.title: Lesotho Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: Water exports to South Africa generate essential revenue but deepen dependence on Pretoria and expose Maseru to disputes over pricing, project delays, and control of downstream infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Textile and Investment Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: The apparel sector remains sensitive to external trade preferences and foreign-owned supply chains, limiting domestic value capture and increasing exposure to shifts in U.S., Chinese, and South African policy.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore and gold expansion is led by foreign investors, leaving Liberia dependent on concession terms, export infrastructure, and external capital while local processing remains limited.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Influence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign operators and financiers retain substantial influence over ports, rail links, and mining corridors, creating recurring sovereignty concerns over revenue transparency and strategic access.

frictionVectors.title: Competing Oil Authorities
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and security networks continue to contest control over the National Oil Corporation, terminals, and revenue flows, allowing external actors to shape production and budget access.

frictionVectors.title: Turkish and Russian Security Footprints
frictionVectors.details: Turkey and Russia maintain influential military and political positions through local partners, constraining Libya's autonomous security policy and increasing the risk that energy infrastructure becomes a bargaining tool.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Value-Chain Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and graphite projects remain dominated by foreign capital and export-oriented infrastructure, with Madagascar capturing relatively limited downstream value and fiscal leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Maritime Access
frictionVectors.details: Gulf, Chinese, Indian, and Western actors are competing for influence around ports, logistics, and offshore resources, raising concerns about strategic concessions and weak regulatory capacity.

highlights: Critical Minerals Move Up the Agenda

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The planned restart of Kayelekera uranium and interest in rare earths could improve export earnings, but foreign operators retain substantial financing and technical leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Fuel and Foreign-Exchange Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF-backed reforms are easing pressure, yet fuel imports, donor financing, and foreign-exchange shortages continue to constrain policy autonomy.

highlights: Sahel Sovereignty Tied to Russian Security Support

frictionVectors.title: Barrick Gold Confrontation
frictionVectors.details: Bamako is pressing international mining firms for a larger state share of gold revenues, creating legal, operational, and investor-confidence risks.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Security cooperation with Russia-linked forces has reduced reliance on Western partners but increases external influence over counterinsurgency policy and strategic infrastructure.

highlights: Offshore Gas Enters the Strategic Equation
Iron Ore State Capacity Gradually Expands

frictionVectors.title: Greater Tortue Ahmeyim Governance
frictionVectors.details: The Senegal-linked offshore gas project offers new leverage and revenue, but dependence on BP, Kosmos, and cross-border operating arrangements limits unilateral control.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Led Green Hydrogen Corridors
frictionVectors.details: Large renewable-hydrogen proposals could transform infrastructure and exports, while requiring extensive foreign capital, land allocation, and port development.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos and Diego Garcia
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius continues to pursue sovereignty over the Chagos Archipelago while the Diego Garcia military facility remains central to wider British-American strategic interests.

frictionVectors.title: Port Competition and External Capital
frictionVectors.details: Expansion of maritime and logistics infrastructure is economically valuable but exposes Mauritius to competing Indian, Chinese, and Western influence in the Indian Ocean.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Recognition Contest
frictionVectors.details: Morocco uses control and development of the territory to reinforce sovereignty claims, while the dispute continues to shape relations with Algeria, the EU, and international investors.

frictionVectors.title: Green Hydrogen and Water Stress
frictionVectors.details: Renewable-energy and desalination projects strengthen Morocco's strategic autonomy, but they require foreign technology and capital amid mounting domestic water scarcity.

highlights: Cabo Delgado Remains a Sovereignty Test

frictionVectors.title: Foreign LNG Concessions
frictionVectors.details: International energy firms retain substantial control over the capital-intensive LNG sector. Project security, revenue-sharing, and local-content commitments remain central sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Insurgency
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent violence continues to threaten gas infrastructure and state authority. Reliance on foreign security assistance exposes Mozambique to external leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Offshore Energy
frictionVectors.details: International firms dominate early-stage offshore oil development, creating future disputes over fiscal terms, local participation, and environmental risk.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: External investors are competing for uranium, lithium, and green-hydrogen opportunities. Namibia is seeking stronger domestic processing and strategic leverage before projects scale.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The military government is pressing foreign mining interests for greater state control and revenue. Operational uncertainty and diplomatic disputes threaten investment and export continuity.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Export Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Niger relies heavily on cross-border infrastructure to move crude to global markets. Political tensions with neighbors and insecurity along transport routes constrain effective sovereignty over the sector.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline Theft and Sabotage
frictionVectors.details: Crude theft, vandalism, and illegal refining continue to reduce state revenues and weaken regulatory control. Security failures also discourage investment in upstream and midstream infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital and Divestment
frictionVectors.details: International oil companies remain important, even as some sell mature onshore assets to domestic operators. The transition could strengthen local ownership but also shift liabilities and technical risks to the state.

frictionVectors.title: Great Lakes Mineral Supply Chains
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda is a major trading and processing hub for minerals from the Great Lakes region. International scrutiny over traceability and alleged links between regional conflict and mineral flows creates persistent reputational and diplomatic pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Congo Security Entanglement
frictionVectors.details: Tensions involving armed groups and neighboring states complicate cross-border commerce and regional infrastructure. Security partnerships and diplomatic pressure limit Kigali's room for maneuver despite strong internal state control.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore resource uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: Prospective hydrocarbon blocks attract foreign interest, but weak institutional capacity and uncertain commercial viability limit São Tomé and Príncipe's bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Gulf of Guinea dependence
frictionVectors.details: The country relies on external partners for maritime surveillance and port-related investment, creating sovereignty risks around its waters and logistics infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign energy operators
frictionVectors.details: New oil and gas production offers major fiscal upside, but contracts, operators and export infrastructure leave Dakar balancing investor confidence against stronger local-content and revenue demands.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic realignment
frictionVectors.details: The government's push for greater autonomy is reducing France's political primacy while increasing scrutiny of Gulf, Chinese and Turkish financing and infrastructure proposals.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign fishing access
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles gains revenue and food-security benefits from distant-water fishing, but foreign access and transshipment arrangements can constrain control over marine resources.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic infrastructure competition
frictionVectors.details: India, China, Gulf states and Western partners compete for influence through maritime security, finance and connectivity projects, requiring careful sovereignty management.

frictionVectors.title: Iron-ore and mining dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale mining remains central to export earnings, but foreign ownership, tax concessions and local environmental impacts limit domestic control over value chains.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor influence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed port, road and logistics projects could improve national connectivity while creating long-term dependence on external capital and commodity-linked concessions.

frictionVectors.title: External security architecture
frictionVectors.details: Somalia remains dependent on foreign military, financial and diplomatic support to contain al-Shabaab, limiting the federal government's effective control over territory, ports and maritime approaches.

frictionVectors.title: Ports and offshore hydrocarbons
frictionVectors.details: Turkish, Gulf and other foreign actors are deeply involved in port and security arrangements, while offshore oil prospects risk reproducing externally controlled concessions before national institutions are consolidated.

highlights: Grid and port bottlenecks constrain leverage

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is seeking greater domestic beneficiation and supply-chain control, while Chinese, Western, and Gulf investors compete for access to platinum-group metals, manganese, and energy-transition minerals.

frictionVectors.title: Electricity and logistics strain
frictionVectors.details: Grid instability, rail congestion, and underperforming ports weaken sovereign control over mineral exports and increase dependence on private capital and external technical partners.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-export corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan relies on Sudanese pipelines and Red Sea infrastructure to monetize its oil, leaving revenues exposed to conflict, transit disruption, and bargaining by external security and commercial actors.

frictionVectors.title: Elite capture and armed fragmentation
frictionVectors.details: Political rivalries and localized violence limit transparent management of oil income, land, and humanitarian supply chains, reinforcing dependence on foreign donors and neighboring states.

highlights: War fragments control of strategic assets
Red Sea access attracts competing powers

frictionVectors.title: Gold and war-finance networks
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and cross-border trading remain central to financing rival armed actors, with Gulf-linked commercial networks and regional intermediaries shaping access to Sudanese resources.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Control of Port Sudan, pipelines, and agricultural corridors is strategically contested, while foreign military, commercial, and diplomatic actors seek influence over Red Sea access.

highlights: Resource nationalism paired with investment pragmatism
LNG and corridor projects expand strategic weight

frictionVectors.title: LNG bargaining and local-content pressure
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is pursuing long-delayed offshore gas development while demanding stronger state participation, revenue guarantees, and local benefits from international energy companies.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Rail, port, and power expansion is improving national connectivity, but financing and construction partnerships with China, Gulf investors, and other external actors create long-term leverage over strategic infrastructure.

highlights: Lomé strengthens its regional logistics role
Security pressures reach the northern frontier

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics influence
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé remains a key Gulf of Guinea transshipment and commercial hub, but its growth increases exposure to foreign operators, shipping interests, and regional trade competition.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel spillover
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist violence and instability in northern Togo and neighboring Burkina Faso are driving reliance on external security cooperation while threatening transport corridors and agricultural livelihoods.

frictionVectors.title: EU migration bargain
frictionVectors.details: European funding and political pressure over migration management give Brussels significant leverage over Tunisia's security and fiscal choices. Tunis resists being treated primarily as Europe's migration gatekeeper while remaining dependent on external financing.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and phosphate strain
frictionVectors.details: Natural-gas import dependence and declining phosphate output constrain industrial sovereignty. Delays in energy investment and infrastructure modernization leave the country exposed to price shocks and foreign creditors.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP financing pressure
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania oil pipeline remains central to Kampala's resource strategy but faces Western environmental, legal, and financing opposition. Chinese and Gulf-linked capital offer alternatives, while construction risks and compensation disputes remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-backed infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese involvement in roads, energy, and oil infrastructure expands Uganda's room for maneuver but increases repayment and collateral concerns. Kampala is balancing strategic autonomy against concentrated external financing exposure.

frictionVectors.title: Copper ownership contest
frictionVectors.details: Lusaka is courting Gulf, American, Chinese, and European partners to expand copper and critical-minerals production while seeking greater domestic value addition. The resulting competition improves bargaining power but risks renewed disputes over tax, royalties, and operational control.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito Corridor offers a strategic route to Atlantic markets and reduces reliance on southern and eastern African corridors. Its success depends on large external infrastructure commitments, leaving Zambia exposed to geopolitical competition and implementation delays.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Harare is using export restrictions and local-processing demands to capture more value from lithium, platinum, gold, and diamonds. Chinese investment remains influential, but the government is trying to diversify partners without surrendering control over strategic deposits.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and payment risk
frictionVectors.details: Sanctions exposure, weak correspondent banking access, and currency instability raise transaction costs across mining and infrastructure projects. These constraints push Zimbabwe toward opaque or politically aligned financing channels and reduce effective sovereign bargaining power.
